title: How Soccer Works
summary: Josh Clark and Chuck Bryant explain how soccer works for American listeners ahead of the World Cup. They cover ancient ball games (Chinese cuju, Japanese kemari, Mesoamerican ballgame, English village football), the 1863-era split of association football from rugby and the origin of the word "soccer," the codification of rules by FIFA and the referee and field changes, the history and format of the World Cup (qualifying, group play, tiebreakers, knockout rounds, penalty shootouts), basic gameplay (positions, formations, set pieces, cards, offside), diving and gamesmanship, the English Premier League and relegation, MLS, and hooliganism. The episode ends with listener mail about nurses and prescribers.

segments.title: Opening banter and childhood soccer experiences
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Chuck's vacation, the Miami Heat, and their experiences playing soccer as kids.

segments.title: Soccer's similarity to other ball games and ancient origins
segments.summary: The hosts compare soccer to hockey, American football and basketball, then describe ancient ball games: Mesoamerican ballgame (pok-ta-pok/popham), Chinese cuju, and Japanese kemari.

segments.title: Medieval English village football and the origin of soccer
segments.summary: Village football in England was banned from the 13th to 17th centuries and later schoolkids formalized the rules. The hosts discuss how the word soccer came from association football, and the 1848 Cambridge meeting that split rugby from soccer.

segments.title: Evolution of rules, FIFA, and the field
segments.summary: The hosts describe how FIFA was founded in 1904, how goal kicks, corner kicks, a single referee, penalties and the field layout were introduced, and how rules still change, such as the offside line change.

segments.title: World Cup history and Americans' interest
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck discuss Americans' lukewarm interest in soccer and World Cup fever. They recount the first World Cup in 1930 hosted by Uruguay, and that hosts are guaranteed entry.

segments.title: World Cup qualifying, groups and tiebreakers
segments.summary: The hosts explain regional qualifying slots, the play-in for Oceania, seeding into eight groups of four, three points for a win, the group of death including the US, and tiebreakers by point differential and goals scored.

segments.title: Knockout rounds and penalty shootouts
segments.summary: The knockout stage is single elimination with no ties. Penalty shootouts decide tied games, and the hosts describe penalty kick distance and goalkeeper rules, plus the historical change in penalty placement before 1902.

segments.title: Basic gameplay, positions and formations
segments.summary: The hosts explain the basics: eleven players per side, goals, goalkeeper handball in the box, halves, stoppage time, positions of defenders, midfielders and forwards, formations like 4-4-2, and the meaning of marking and tackling.

segments.title: Set pieces, cards, free kicks and walls
segments.summary: The hosts describe throw-ins, goal kicks, corner kicks, direct and indirect free kicks, the defensive wall, and yellow and red cards.

segments.title: Diving, flopping and gamesmanship
segments.summary: The hosts discuss diving and exaggerated injuries, cultural differences in attitudes toward gamesmanship, and the 1989 Chile-Brazil qualifier in which goalkeeper Roberto Rojas injured himself to get Brazil disqualified; Brazil later offered him a job. They also mention basketball flopping.

segments.title: Offside rule
segments.summary: The hosts explain the offside rule: an attacker is offside if closer to the goal line than the last defender when the ball is played to them in regular play, not on restarts.

segments.title: Premier League, relegation, MLS and hooliganism
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the English Premier League and relegation, MLS, aging players moving to the US, and soccer hooliganism and crowd crushes.
